title: Overriding a method
summary: CheckingAccount replaces withdraw with its own rules.

say.never: `@Override` means "this method **replaces** the parent's version". A checking account has different withdrawing rules (it allows an overdraft), so it writes its own `withdraw`. Everything else, like `deposit` and `transfer`, still works exactly as before.
say.bit: `@Override` says this method **replaces** the parent's version. Everything else (deposit, transfer) still works as before.

marks.label: can go negative, but only this far

say.never: Here's the clever part. `transfer` was written in `BankAccount`, long before checking accounts existed. But when you call it on a checking account, it uses the **overridden** `withdraw`. Java picks the version that belongs to the real object. That's the power of inheritance.
say.bit: `transfer` was written in BankAccount, but on a checking account it calls the **overridden** withdraw. That's the power of inheritance.
